title: NFTs & Digital Ownership
tagline: Understand how NFTs work, what you really own and how to trade them safely.

modules.title: What is an NFT?
modules.summary: An NFT is a unique token on a blockchain that records who owns a specific item. This module explains what makes NFTs different from regular tokens.
objectives: Explain the difference between fungible and non-fungible tokens
Describe what an NFT records on the blockchain
List common uses for NFTs beyond art

sections.heading: Fungible and non-fungible
sections.body: Fungible means interchangeable: one dollar or one ETH is as good as any other. Non-fungible means each item is unique, like a concert seat with its own row and number. NFT stands for non-fungible token, a token that cannot be swapped one-for-one with another.

sections.heading: What an NFT records
sections.body: Each NFT lives in a smart contract and has its own token ID. The blockchain records which address owns each ID and keeps a public history of every transfer. Anyone can check who owns a given NFT and where it came from.

sections.heading: More than pictures
sections.body: NFTs are well known for digital art, but the same idea works for many things. Examples include event tickets, game items, membership passes, domain names and certificates. In each case the NFT acts as a verifiable record of ownership.

concepts.definition: Interchangeable, where every unit is worth the same as any other unit.
A unique token on a blockchain that cannot be swapped one-for-one with another.
The number that identifies one specific NFT inside its contract.
The full ownership history of an item, back to when it was created.

example.title: An NFT concert ticket
example.body: A venue sells tickets as NFTs. Each ticket has its own token ID tied to a seat. At the door, staff check that the holder's wallet owns that token ID. Because the history is public, a buyer on a resale market can confirm the ticket came from the venue's official contract.

modules.title: Token standards and metadata
modules.summary: NFTs follow shared standards so wallets and marketplaces can read them. This module covers ERC-721, ERC-1155 and where the image and details are actually stored.
objectives: Explain how tokenURI and metadata work
Describe the trade-offs of different storage options

sections.heading: ERC-721
sections.body: ERC-721 is the original Ethereum standard for NFTs. Each token ID in an ERC-721 contract is unique and has exactly one owner. Functions such as ownerOf and transferFrom work the same way across every compliant contract, so any wallet or marketplace can support them.

sections.heading: ERC-1155
sections.body: ERC-1155 is a multi-token standard. One contract can hold many token types, and each type can have one copy or many copies. This suits games, where a contract might hold a unique sword alongside thousands of identical potions. It also supports batch transfers, which save gas when moving several items at once.

sections.heading: Metadata and tokenURI
sections.body: Most NFTs do not store their image on-chain. Instead, the contract returns a link, called the tokenURI, that points to a JSON file with the name, description, attributes and image link. Wallets and marketplaces read this file to display the NFT.

sections.heading: Where files are stored
sections.body: If metadata sits on an ordinary web server, the owner of that server can change or delete it. IPFS uses content addressing, where the link is a hash of the file, so the content behind a link cannot change, though someone must keep pinning it. Some projects store everything fully on-chain, which costs more but removes outside dependencies.

concepts.definition: The Ethereum standard for unique NFTs, where each token ID has one owner.
A multi-token standard where one contract can hold both unique and identical tokens.
A link returned by an NFT contract that points to the token's metadata.
Identifying a file by a hash of its content, so the link always means the same data.

example.title: A game item contract
example.body: A game uses one ERC-1155 contract for its items. Token type 1 is a legendary shield with a supply of one. Token type 2 is a healing potion with a supply of fifty thousand. A player can send three potions and the shield to a friend in one batch transfer.

modules.title: Ownership, rights and royalties
modules.summary: Owning an NFT is not the same as owning everything about the artwork. This module covers licences, royalties, approvals and the safety risks of trading NFTs.
objectives: Separate token ownership from copyright and licence rights
Explain how ERC-2981 royalties work and their limits

sections.heading: Token versus rights
sections.body: Owning an NFT means your address controls that token. It does not automatically give you the copyright to the artwork. What you may do with the art, such as commercial use, depends on the licence the creator attaches, which can range from none to very broad.

sections.heading: Royalties
sections.body: ERC-2981 is a standard that lets an NFT contract report a royalty amount and recipient for each sale. It only reports the information: it cannot force a marketplace to pay. Whether creators receive royalties depends on each marketplace's policy or on extra transfer restrictions built into the contract.

sections.heading: Marketplace approvals
sections.body: To list NFTs, you usually call setApprovalForAll, which lets an operator move every NFT you hold in that collection. That is convenient for real marketplaces but dangerous if the operator is malicious. Drainers often ask for this approval, and it should be revoked when no longer needed.

sections.heading: Fakes and copies
sections.body: Anyone can deploy a contract with the same name and images as a famous collection. The only reliable check is the contract address. Verify it from the project's official channels before buying, rather than trusting a name or a picture.

concepts.definition: The terms that state what an NFT holder may legally do with the underlying work.
A standard that lets an NFT contract report royalty information for sales.
A function that lets an operator move all of your NFTs in one collection.
The on-chain address that uniquely identifies an NFT collection.

example.title: Two identical collections
example.body: Nina finds a cheap listing for a well-known collection. The name and images match, but the contract address differs from the one on the project's official site. She realises it is a copycat contract. Checking the address saved her from buying a worthless copy.

modules.title: Mint mechanics and advanced design
modules.summary: Behind a smooth mint sit careful design choices. This module covers allowlists with Merkle proofs, lazy minting, fair reveals and soulbound tokens.
objectives: Explain how Merkle proofs verify allowlists cheaply
Describe lazy minting with signed vouchers
Understand fair reveals and non-transferable tokens

sections.heading: Allowlists with Merkle proofs
sections.body: Storing thousands of allowlisted addresses on-chain is expensive. Instead, a project builds a Merkle tree of the list and stores only its root in the contract. At mint time, each user submits a short proof showing their address is in the tree, and the contract checks it against the root.

sections.heading: Lazy minting
sections.body: With lazy minting, a creator signs a voucher off-chain describing the NFT and its price. Nothing is minted until a buyer submits the voucher, and the buyer pays the gas. The contract checks the creator's signature before minting, so the creator avoids upfront costs.

sections.heading: Fair reveals
sections.body: If buyers can see which token ID will be rare before minting, they can target it. Many projects hide metadata until the mint ends, then reveal it using a random offset. The randomness should come from a source that the team and miners or validators cannot easily predict or bias.

sections.heading: Soulbound tokens
sections.body: A soulbound token is an NFT that cannot be transferred once issued. It suits things that should stay with one person, such as credentials, attendance proofs or reputation. Because it cannot be sold, it represents something earned rather than something bought.

concepts.definition: A single hash that summarises every entry in a Merkle tree.
A short list of hashes that proves one entry belongs to a tree with a known root.
Deferring the mint until a buyer submits a creator-signed voucher.
A non-transferable token tied permanently to one address.

example.title: An allowlist for ten thousand wallets
example.body: A project allowlists ten thousand addresses. Rather than store them all, it saves one Merkle root in the contract. When Kai mints, the website gives him a proof of about fourteen hashes. The contract hashes his address with the proof, gets the stored root and lets him mint.

questions.prompt: What does non-fungible mean?
options: Each item is unique and not interchangeable
Each item is worth exactly the same amount
Each item can be split into smaller parts
Each item is stored outside the blockchain
questions.explanation: Non-fungible items are unique. One cannot be swapped one-for-one with another as if they were identical.

questions.prompt: Which of these is fungible?
options: A numbered concert seat
A one-of-a-kind painting
A unique game character
One unit of a currency
questions.explanation: Currency units are interchangeable, so they are fungible. The other items are each unique.

questions.prompt: What identifies one specific NFT inside its contract?
options: Its market price
Its token ID
Its file size
Its image colour
questions.explanation: Each NFT in a contract has its own token ID, and the contract records who owns each ID.

questions.prompt: Why can a buyer check an NFT's provenance?
options: Because sellers must upload a paper receipt
Because marketplaces keep private sale records
Because transfers are recorded publicly on-chain
Because each NFT image contains a hidden signature
questions.explanation: Every transfer is recorded on the blockchain, so anyone can trace an NFT back to the contract that created it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common non-art use of NFTs?
options: Mining new blocks
Event tickets
Setting gas prices
Storing seed phrases
questions.explanation: NFTs work well as tickets because each one is unique and its ownership is easy to verify.

questions.prompt: What is a key feature of ERC-1155 compared with ERC-721?
options: It only supports a single token per contract
It cannot be traded on any NFT marketplace
One contract can hold unique and identical tokens
It stores every image directly inside the token contract
questions.explanation: ERC-1155 is a multi-token standard. One contract can manage many token types, each with one or many copies.

questions.prompt: What does the tokenURI of an NFT usually point to?
options: A JSON file with the NFT's metadata
The private key of the NFT's owner
The marketplace where it was first sold
The gas fee paid to mint the token
questions.explanation: The tokenURI links to a metadata file with the name, description, attributes and image link.

questions.prompt: In an ERC-721 contract, how many owners can a single token ID have at once?
options: As many as the creator allows
Up to ten addresses at a time
One for each marketplace listing
Exactly one owner
questions.explanation: ERC-721 tokens are unique, and ownerOf returns a single owner for each token ID.

questions.prompt: Why is IPFS often preferred over an ordinary web server for NFT metadata?
options: IPFS files are always stored for free forever by the network
Links are content hashes, so the data cannot change
IPFS automatically pays royalties to creators
Web servers cannot serve image files to wallets
questions.explanation: IPFS links are derived from the file's hash, so the content behind a link cannot be swapped. Someone still has to keep it pinned.

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of ERC-1155 batch transfers?
options: They hide transfers from block explorers
They let anyone mint new tokens for free
They move several items in one transaction
They make every token in the batch unique
questions.explanation: A batch transfer sends several token types in a single transaction, which saves gas compared with separate transfers.

questions.prompt: You buy an NFT of an artwork. What determines whether you can use the art commercially?
options: The price you paid for the NFT
The licence the creator attached
The blockchain it was minted on
The number of NFTs in your wallet
questions.explanation: Token ownership does not transfer copyright by itself. Usage rights come from the creator's licence.

questions.prompt: What does ERC-2981 actually do?
options: It forces every marketplace to pay creator royalties on resale
It stops NFTs from being sold below the mint price
It reports royalty details that marketplaces may honour
It sends royalties automatically on every transfer
questions.explanation: ERC-2981 only reports a royalty amount and recipient. Payment depends on the marketplace or extra contract rules.

questions.prompt: Why is signing setApprovalForAll for an unknown operator risky?
options: It lets the operator move every NFT you hold in that collection
It lets the operator change the artwork in your NFTs
It lets the operator read your private key from the wallet extension
It lets the operator mint new NFTs in your name
questions.explanation: setApprovalForAll grants transfer rights over all your tokens in that collection, which a malicious operator can use to take them.

questions.prompt: What is the most reliable way to confirm an NFT belongs to the real collection?
options: Check that the name matches the famous project
Check that the image looks like the originals
Check that the listing price seems fair
Check the contract address from official sources
questions.explanation: Names and images can be copied, but the contract address is unique. Verify it from the project's official channels.

questions.prompt: If NFT metadata is hosted on a project's own web server, what risk does the holder face?
options: The server owner can change or remove what the NFT shows
The token ID can be reassigned to a different contract by anyone
The holder must pay rent to the server every month
The NFT will be burned if the server is restarted
questions.explanation: The on-chain token stays, but what it displays depends on the server. The owner of the server can alter or delete the data.

questions.prompt: Why do projects store a Merkle root instead of the full allowlist on-chain?
options: It hides who minted from the block explorer
It lets anyone add themselves to the list
It removes the need for any user signature
It costs far less storage while staying verifiable
questions.explanation: One root replaces thousands of stored addresses. Each user proves membership with a short Merkle proof checked against it.

questions.prompt: In lazy minting, who usually pays the gas to create the NFT?
options: The creator, before listing it
The buyer, when submitting the voucher
The marketplace, from its fee income
The validator who includes the block
questions.explanation: The creator signs a voucher off-chain. The NFT is minted only when a buyer submits it, and the buyer pays the gas.

questions.prompt: Why do many collections delay revealing metadata until after the mint?
options: To lower the gas cost of each mint transaction
To make the NFTs non-transferable until the mint has sold out
To stop minters from targeting known rare token IDs
To let the team change the total supply later
questions.explanation: If rarity is visible in advance, buyers can snipe rare IDs. A later reveal with unbiased randomness keeps the mint fair.

questions.prompt: What does a Merkle proof contain?
options: The sibling hashes needed to rebuild the root
Every address on the full allowlist
The private key of the project owner
A signed copy of the NFT's metadata
questions.explanation: A proof lists the sibling hashes along the path from a leaf to the root. Hashing them in order should reproduce the stored root.

questions.prompt: Which use case suits a soulbound token best?
options: A collectible meant to be resold for profit
A game item players trade with each other
A course completion credential for one person
A ticket that fans can pass on to friends
questions.explanation: Soulbound tokens cannot be transferred, which fits records that should stay with one person, like a credential.
